agent_notes: The Hebrew verse 1 includes the superscription (KJV 120:0), so the literal layer carries both title and cry. 'Ascents' (maʿalot) is rendered by its root sense; the three ancient explanations (temple steps, pilgrim ascents, return from exile) are in the commentary, with Rashi, Radak and Meiri cited from the packet.

ויענני is a wayyiqtol after a perfect: 'I called … and he answered'. Radak (on the verse) reads it as past standing for future. I kept the plain past, which is what KJV, ASV and YLT-like readings also do, apart from YLT's present 'answereth'.

agent_notes: Reviewer request applied: the oath-formula claim is now offered as a possible echo of the 'may God do so to you and more also' pattern, with no source. Rashi (God as the giver; 'add' = guards and partitions, citing Arakhin 15b) and Metzudat David (what further guard could be set on you, since you already lie behind the wall of lips and teeth) are described as they read.

The subject of yitten and yosif is unexpressed (3ms). Rashi takes it as God; the KJV, ASV and Webster use impersonal passives; YLT and BBE say 'He'. I kept the Hebrew's open subject in the literal layer ('will [one] give') and used 'He' in the dramatic layer, following the reading shared by Rashi, YLT and BBE and the context of v.2 (the LORD is addressed).

Gloss 3 (lekha) carries the masculine ending and gloss 6 (lakh) the feminine, as in the packet's morphology; the tongue (lashon) is grammatically feminine here, which suits lakh. The shift is odd and I kept both as 'to you' without forcing an explanation. STEPBible's 'will anyone give' and 'will anyone add' were changed to the plain 'he will give' / 'he will add', since 'anyone' presumes the impersonal reading.

agent_notes: Meshech and Kedar are about a thousand miles apart (Anatolia/Black Sea region versus the Arabian desert), so the line is not a literal address; Rashi, Radak, Ibn Ezra and Meiri each take it as exile among nations. The 'figure of speech' reading is Meiri's alternative; the interpretation that the poet is a long-distance sojourner in two extremes is my own wording.
STEPBible glosses אָהֳלֵי קֵדָר as 'tents of Kedar' with entity person.kedar; the packet's Names section calls Kedar a tribe. I glossed it as the name only.

agent_notes: רַבַּת is feminine adjective 'much/long' used adverbially; Ibn Ezra and Radak note the final tav as standing for he. I render 'much' in the literal layer and 'long' in the dramatic layer. לָּהּ is an ethical dative, glossed '[for] herself'.

The syntax of the last line is deliberately compressed in Hebrew: 'I [am] peace, and when I speak, they [are] for war.' Radak, Rashi and Metzudat David take the speech to be words of peace; Ibn Ezra the same, so 'peace' is bracketed in the literal layer.

«Дрок» (Синодальный: «дроковые угли») для רְתָמִים; в буквальном слое использовано «дрока» тоже. Английское broom (Retama raetam) — именно ракитник/дрок пустыни; название растения нетривиально, проверьте.

agent_notes: Мешех и Кидар: Синодальный перевод пишет «Мосох» (по Септуагинте) и «Кидарские». Для Мешеха выбрана форма «Мешех», как в современных переводах и в списке народов Иафета (Быт 10:2); «Мосох» упомянут в комментарии. «Кидар» совпадает с Синодальным.
